intro: Berlioz’s Symphonie fantastique gives its beloved a melody that will haunt all five movements. Here she first appears in flute and violins, after a slow introduction full of silences and sudden stirrings.

sections.label: Intro · Muted strings, hesitant phrases
sections.mNote: A slow C-minor opening, broken by rests and fermatas

sections.label: A · The beloved’s long melody
sections.mNote: Flute and first violins introduce the idée fixe

sections.label: A′ · Fragments of the beloved’s melody
sections.mNote: Strings and woodwinds exchange pieces of the tune

sections.label: A″ · Strings and brass press on

cues.title: A hesitant beginning
cues.text: Flute and clarinet begin quietly, repeating their notes as other wind voices join them. Muted violins take up a melody full of pauses, its phrases separated by fermatas. The strings repeatedly gather courage and fall silent again.
cues.evidence: Berlioz, Symphonie fantastique, movement I, bars 1–16; Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 1–3: http://www.hberlioz.com/scosupp/symfantas1.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A song survives the fire
cues.text: Berlioz burns his early compositions before leaving for Paris, but one melody stays in his memory. Years later it becomes the violins’ song in this introduction. He originally writes it to words from Florian’s Estelle, while grieving over his own adolescent love.
cues.evidence: Berlioz, Mémoires, chapter 4, describes the romance, its destruction and its reuse without alteration in the Largo: http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/fantasf.htm

cues.title: The “vague des passions”
cues.text: Berlioz’s programme gives the artist a “soul-sickness”: melancholy and joys without cause, before he has ever seen her. The name for it, le vague des passions, comes from “a famous writer” the programme leaves unnamed. He is Chateaubriand.
cues.evidence: Berlioz’s 1845 programme, part I: http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/fantasf.htm . Michel Austin identifies the “famous writer” as Chateaubriand and relates the phrase to the opening of the symphony: http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/sfantastique.htm

cues.title: Beethoven comes to Paris
cues.text: In 1828 Habeneck’s new Conservatoire concerts brought Beethoven to Paris. Berlioz wrote that he “opened a new world in music”. After the C minor Symphony, his teacher Lesueur hurried out red-faced: he was so shaken, he said, that he thought he could not find his head to put his hat on.
cues.evidence: Berlioz, Mémoires, chapter 20 (“Il m’ouvrait un monde nouveau en musique”; Lesueur after the symphony in C minor): https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/M%C3%A9moires_de_Hector_Berlioz/20 . Date of Habeneck’s Beethoven performances: http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/sfantastique.htm

cues.title: Harriet on the Paris stage
cues.text: In September 1827 Berlioz sees Harriet Smithson acting Shakespeare in Paris. He falls in love before they have met. By 1830 he is writing a symphony about an artist haunted by his beloved; Smithson will hear the revised work in December 1832.
cues.evidence: Hector Berlioz Website, Symphonie fantastique, introduction and composition history: Smithson’s 1827 performances and attendance at the concert of 9 December 1832. http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/sfantastique.htm

cues.title: Flute and violins fall in love
cues.text: The flute and first violins sing the idée fixe — the fixed idea, or obsession. Its opening G hangs across the barline before the melody reaches upwards. Long notes and fresh starts carry the phrase far beyond a neat four-bar tune.
cues.evidence: Movement I, bars 71–111, Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 15–17. Berlioz’s 1845 programme identifies this melody with the beloved: http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/fantasf.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Two rehearsals in Paris
cues.text: On 5 December 1830, Habeneck conducts the première at the Paris Conservatoire. The players give their services free. They have only two rehearsals for the new symphony and Berlioz’s cantata Sardanapale. Three movements cause a sensation; the countryside scene barely registers.
cues.evidence: Berlioz, Mémoires, chapter 31, on the première, unpaid players, two rehearsals and the contrasting reception of the movements: http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/fantasf.htm

cues.title: The melody in pieces
cues.text: In the development, the long tune breaks into shorter phrases. Strings begin a figure and woodwinds answer; a held chord can leave the lower strings moving beneath it. The beloved’s melody keeps returning in these scraps of conversation.
cues.evidence: Movement I, development from bar 168, Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 27–39. The thematic development is discussed at http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/sfantastique.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The beloved’s earlier voice
cues.text: The idée fixe already exists in Berlioz’s 1828 cantata Herminie, written for the Prix de Rome. He takes a melody first heard in a vocal work and gives it to the orchestra. It will survive a waltz, an execution and a witches’ dance.
cues.evidence: Hector Berlioz Website, Symphonie fantastique, composition history, identifies the borrowing from Herminie; the programme describes the melody’s later appearances. http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/sfantastique.htm

cues.title: Strings against brass chords
cues.text: The late Allegro drives quick string phrases against broad wind and brass chords. Trumpets and cornets join the horns, and the violins climb high above them. The score presses from forte to fortissimo.
cues.evidence: Movement I, late Allegro, including bars 403–424; Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 54–58, shows the climbing strings and sustained wind-and-brass chords.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Chords like a quiet prayer
cues.text: Religiosamente. Woodwinds, horns and strings hold broad chords, marked pianississimo. Trumpets and cornets fall silent. In the programme, the artist finds religious consolation; in the score, the restless string figures have finally stopped.
cues.evidence: Movement I, bars 513–525, Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 71–72; Berlioz’s 1845 programme ends its first-movement account with religious consolation. http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/fantasf.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A held G begins the obsession
transitions.how: The score changes to C major and Allegro agitato e appassionato assai. After emphatic chords, the strings soften and the bass moves downwards. Flute and first violins begin the idée fixe on G; that note hangs across a barline before the melody rises to C and E.
transitions.evidence: Movement I, bars 64–76, Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 14–15: tempo change, descending bass and first statement of the idée fixe. http://www.hberlioz.com/scosupp/symfantas1.pdf

transitions.title: The orchestra holds a quiet chord
transitions.from: A″ · Strings and brass press on
transitions.how: The strings’ moving phrases slow and settle. At Religiosamente, woodwinds, horns and strings hold a succession of quiet chords, marked pianississimo. The timpani punctuate the bass while trumpets and cornets remain silent. The closing progression settles in C major.
transitions.evidence: Movement I, bars 497 to the end, with Religiosamente from bar 513; Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 70–72.

source.title: Berlioz, Symphonie fantastique I — orchestral score
source.locator: Largo introduction; first full idée fixe, bars 71–111; development from bar 168; late Allegro; Religiosamente from bar 513.

timeline.note: Flute and clarinet begin the repeated notes; oboe, bassoons and horns join the opening phrase.
Muted first violins sing above the other strings, with pauses between their phrases.
Wind phrases answer the strings as the slow introduction grows more animated.
Flute and first violins introduce the idée fixe above a quiet string accompaniment.
Strings and woodwinds exchange fragments of the long melody.
Quick string phrases climb against wind and brass chords.
Quiet winds, horns and strings hold the Religiosamente chords, with occasional timpani strokes. Piccolo joins the final three bars; trumpets and cornets stay silent.

composer.background:
When the young Hector Berlioz read aloud the death of Dido, his voice failed him. His father closed the book and announced that he was tired, allowing the boy to escape without having to explain his tears. Berlioz remembered the kindness in his Mémoires. Louis Berlioz was a doctor in La Côte-Saint-André, between Lyon and Grenoble, and taught his son Latin, history and geography. He expected Hector to follow him into medicine. The boy learnt flute and guitar, pored over maps of distant islands and took Virgil’s abandoned queen personally.

In 1821 he went to Paris to study medicine. His first visit to the dissecting room at the Pitié hospital, he later wrote, ended with a flight through a window. On the second visit he managed perfectly well. Music was the more durable obstacle. He heard Salieri’s Les Danaïdes at the Opéra and began singing its airs over the cadavers. At the Conservatoire library he copied and memorised Gluck’s scores. His father argued, threatened and withheld support. Hector took composition lessons with Jean-François Le Sueur.
